title: Carbon cycle and climate change; Evidence for evolution
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EC05b#t1 term and clue written for the game; EC05b#t2 term and clue written for the game; EC05a#t2 term and clue written for the game; EC05a#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EC05a#N.5a, EC05b#N.3, EC05c#N.2, EV03b#N.12, EC05a#N.9, EC05b#N.5, EC05c#N.7, EC05a#N.12, EC05b#N.15, EC05c#N.16.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Infrared
items.clue: The radiation given off by the warm surface of the Earth

items.label: Methane
items.clue: Gas rising from ruminant livestock, rice paddies and landfill

items.label: Respiration
items.clue: Process in every organism, producers included, that returns CO₂

items.label: Photosynthesis
items.clue: Process that removes CO₂ from air or water and fixes it in producers

questions.stem: In an experiment, all the decomposers in a woodland soil are killed, but the trees keep growing for a while. Which change would follow over the next few years?

options.text: Dead leaves would pile up and the soil would run short of ions such as phosphate, so growth would slow.
Nothing would change, because elements are released from dead leaves automatically as they fall.
Only carbon recycling would stop; nitrogen and phosphorus would return to the soil as before.
The trees would lose their energy supply, because decomposers return energy from dead leaves to plants.

questions.stem: At Mauna Loa, atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration rises to a peak each May and falls to a minimum each September or October, a swing of several parts per million. What causes this annual fluctuation?

options.text: People burn more fuel for heating in the Northern Hemisphere winter, so combustion raises carbon dioxide until spring and it falls again in summer.
Plants respire only in winter, when they cannot photosynthesise, so carbon dioxide is released only in the cold months and absorbed in the warm months.
In the Northern Hemisphere growing season photosynthesis exceeds respiration, drawing carbon dioxide down; in autumn and winter respiration exceeds photosynthesis.
Biological processes are too small to change the whole atmosphere, so the regular swing must be an artefact of the measuring instruments at the observatory.

questions.stem: The bird species of a mountain in New Guinea were surveyed in 1965 and again in 2012. For most species both the upper and the lower limits of the altitudinal range had moved upslope, by about 100 m on average, over a period in which the region warmed. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The species have expanded their ranges, since they now occupy about 100 m more of the mountain.
Because both limits moved equally, the species have lost none of their habitat area.
The correlation between warming and the shift proves that no other factor was involved.
The ranges of the species shifted upslope, tracking the rise in temperature.

questions.stem: The amino acid sequence of the same protein was compared in four species. Compared with species W, species X differs at 2 positions, species Y at 15 positions and species Z at 31 positions. Which conclusion is supported by the data?

options.text: W shares a more recent common ancestor with X than it does with either Y or Z.
Z is the most primitive of the four species, because its sequence is furthest from W's.
X lives in the same kind of habitat as W, because similar conditions give similar proteins.
X is the ancestor of W, because the two sequences are almost identical.

questions.explanation: Differences accumulate after two lineages split. W and X differ least, so their common ancestor is the most recent.

questions.stem: Which statement about the combustion of biomass, peat, coal, oil and natural gas is correct?

options.text: All formed from organisms at about the same time in the distant past, so burning any of them has the same significance for the carbon cycle.
Burning biomass such as wood releases no carbon dioxide because it is renewable, whereas burning the fossil fuels does release it.
All release carbon dioxide that was originally fixed by photosynthesis, at dates ranging from recent years to hundreds of millions of years ago.
Coal, oil and natural gas release carbon of mineral origin that did not come from living organisms, unlike biomass and peat.

questions.explanation: Biomass may be a few years old, peat thousands of years, coal, oil and gas millions; all began as carbon fixed by autotrophs.

questions.stem: Which is an anthropogenic cause of the rise in the atmospheric concentration of methane since pre-industrial times?

options.text: Enteric fermentation in the growing numbers of ruminant farm livestock
Exhalation of waste gases by the greatly increased human population
Complete combustion of coal and petroleum in vehicles and power stations
Escape of ancient methane trapped in bubbles in melting polar ice

questions.explanation: Methanogenic archaea in the guts of cattle and other ruminants release methane, and livestock numbers have risen greatly.

questions.stem: In the illustrative results in N.6, few eggs hatched at 15 °C and at 35 °C. Which explanation is best?

options.text: At 15 °C the cold denatured the embryos' enzymes; at 35 °C their enzymes were working at their fastest.
At 15 °C enzyme reactions ran slowly; at 35 °C some enzymes denatured, so development often failed.
Hatching time is fixed by the shrimps' genes, so the differences between temperatures must be due to chance.
At 35 °C the enzymes were only denatured for a while, so those eggs will hatch normally once cooled.

questions.explanation: Low temperature means fewer enzyme–substrate collisions. Above the optimum, enzymes lose their shape and development fails.

questions.stem: A peat bog has stored carbon for thousands of years in waterlogged soil. It is drained for farmland, and the peat dries out. What happens to much of the carbon in the peat?

options.text: Air reaches the peat, so decomposers break it down and respire it, releasing its carbon as CO₂.
It stays locked in the soil, because decomposition moves carbon into the soil rather than out of it.
Drying slows the decay, as wet conditions speed up rotting, so the soil stores even more carbon.
The crops' roots absorb it from the soil and build it into their biomass.

questions.explanation: Waterlogging kept O₂ out and decay slow. Drained, the peat is decomposed and the bog turns from a store into a source of CO₂.

questions.stem: At a monitoring station in Tasmania, in the Southern Hemisphere, carbon dioxide shows a much smaller yearly swing than at Mauna Loa, but a similar long-term rise. Which explanation fits both observations?

options.text: The swing is small because fewer people burn fuel for winter heating there; the rise is because more people breathe out CO₂.
The swing is small because the south has much less land and plant life; the rise is from combustion CO₂ mixing worldwide.
The swing is small because southern plants stop respiring in winter; the rise is because volcanoes have become more active.
Both are measurement errors, because living things are far too small to change the carbon dioxide in the whole atmosphere.

questions.stem: A hypothetical small mammal lives only in cool meadows near the top of an isolated mountain. Over 40 years the region warms by 1.5 °C. Which outcome is most likely?

options.text: Its range expands, because warmer conditions open up more of the mountain to it.
Individuals change their genes to suit the warmer climate, so the species stays where it is.
It loses its lower slopes, and its range shrinks towards the summit.
It moves upslope with no loss, as the same band of temperature is still found higher up.

questions.explanation: The cool band shifts up, but a mountain narrows towards the top, so the area left shrinks. An isolated summit leaves nowhere cooler to go: local extinction is a real risk.
